_readme.what: The frozen interface between the town-square engine and everything that renders it. The viz, lane and asset tracks build against this file; the engine track fills in `ticks` from a real seeded run and must match `expectedTape`.
_readme.ticksAreGenerated: `ticks` is empty here on purpose. Ten ticks of seeded cells come out of mulberry32(fnv1a32(...)) and cannot be hand-written. The engine track generates them and commits them into this same file.
_readme.tickPayload: { turn, agents: { id: { role, cell, facing, goal, mood, plan, mass, belief } }, items: { id: { kind, cell } }, ecology: [...] }. It is spider-fly's own tick payload plus the `items` map and the `role` and `facing` fields.
_readme.role: "predator" or "prey". Keyed by role, never by species, so a new cast is a new roles object and no engine edit.
_readme.cell: A "cell-<x>-<y>" id. x and y both run 1..gridSize.
_readme.facing: One of "north", "south", "east", "west". Never degrees, never null. An agent that held still keeps the facing it had; an agent that has never moved uses defaultFacing.
_readme.goal: The one-sentence goal line, for the HUD card and the chat lane.
_readme.mood: The branch's own mood word, also appended as this turn's mgx:feels fact.
_readme.plan: The direction sequence that produced THIS tick's move: the full search result when findActionPath found one, a length-1 array for a single greedy step, [] when the agent held still. plan[0] is always the direction actually taken, and is what drives facing.
_readme.mass: A number rounded to massPrecision decimal places.
_readme.items: Inert food. `kind` is one of the roles.food kinds. An item has no belief, no goal and no plan; it is a subject with a cell.
_readme.belief: A flat object whose key set is every live agent and item id except the observer's own, sorted, each value a cell-id string or null. null means the observer believes nothing about that subject, which is the difference between this map and ground truth.
_readme.vision: Chebyshev radius, per role, with no line of sight. A prop blocks movement (the world pack omits its mgx:has-exit-* edges) and does not block sight. The predator's radius is larger than the prey's, so there is a band where the predator has acquired something that cannot see it back.
_readme.ecology: A tagged union, `type` first. Shapes: { type: "eat-agent", predator, prey, cell, massGained }; { type: "eat-item", agent, item, cell, massGained }; { type: "starve", agent, cell }; { type: "spawn-food", item, kind, cell, mass }; { type: "spawn-prey", agent, cell, mass }; { type: "place-food", item, kind, cell, mass, placedBy }.
_readme.ecologyOrder: Within one turn the pass runs in a fixed order and the array is in that order: eat-agent, eat-item, starve, spawn-prey, spawn-food. place-food is a player action rather than a pass step, and is appended before the pass runs on the turn the player issues it.
_readme.rungs: expectedTape names the decision rung each agent reached. A predator's chain is avoid (another predator believed) > chase > wander. A prey's chain is evade > forage > wander. An agent that is not on the board for that turn's decisions has no entry.

_designNote.theContractIsTheTape: expectedTape fixes which ecology event types fire on each of the ten turns and which rung every live agent reached. It deliberately fixes no cells: every wander is a seeded pick, so cells are an output of the run, not an input to it.
_designNote.theKnobIsInitial: If a generated run does not match the tape, retune `initial` (starting cells and the prop layout), never the tape and never the config. The tape is what the viz, lane and camera work was written against.
_designNote.whyTheTerrace: house-1/2/3 stand in a column at x=8, y=1..3. It is the fixture's one deliberate piece of level design: a prey backed against it runs out of cells that increase its distance from the predator, holds still because holding still scores as well as anything else, and gets stepped on. That is how turn 9's eat-agent happens without a catch mechanic — a predator and a prey both move one cell a turn, so on open board a chase never closes.
_designNote.whyTheAsymmetryMatters: predatorVisionRadius 4 against preyVisionRadius 3 leaves a one-cell band where the predator has acquired something that cannot see it back. Turn 5 sits in it: the fox is on the chase rung while goblin-1 is still foraging, because goblin-1 believes nothing about the fox. Turn 6 is the band closing — goblin-1 comes inside its own radius, flips to evade, and abandons the food. That pair is the asymmetry doing its work in both directions.
_designNote.whyGoblin3StartsAlmostEmpty: Starvation cannot happen naturally inside ten ticks — 8 mass at 0.06 a turn is 133 turns. goblin-3 is seeded at 0.59, which is 0.05 plus nine turns of drain, so it reads 0.05 going into turn 10 and reaches 0 during it. The brief for this fixture said 0.05; 0.05 alone starves on turn 1, so the nine turns of drain are added to land the starve where the tape wants it. Adjusting the config per tick would have been the worse fix: the config is one frozen table for the whole run. goblin-3 must not eat, so keep it away from wherever food spawns; if a seeded crumb lands on it, retune its start cell.
_designNote.whyTheTrapDoesNotSpring: Turn 8's morsel is placed next to the predator, and turn 10's eat-item is on that same morsel by a different prey. Those are not the same event. A prey close enough to believe a morsel that sits one cell from a predator is always close enough to believe the predator too, so evade always beats forage there and the bait is never taken while the predator stands over it. It gets eaten on turn 10 because the predator has chased something else off the spot. The trap is real, and what it catches is whatever walks in after the predator leaves.
_designNote.tapeRungsCorrected: Turns 5, 6 and 10 originally carried hand-authored rungs that no starting board reaches. The engine track swept 285,000 boards over every fox/prey pair and 400,000 random boards, and hit the original turn-7 requirement zero times: the tape asked the predator to sit at exactly Chebyshev 4 while the prey stood on a seeded crumb cell, having wandered for five turns. All ten ecology arrays matched from the first run, so the events were right and only these three rung annotations were wishful. They now record what the engine reaches.

_rolesNote: The predator is a fox. The design doc says wolf; the wolf model turned out not to be CC0, so the cast changed and this file is the authority.
_propFactsNote: Four rows per prop, and every object is a string — "90", never 90. A fact object is a term, and a renderer that reads mgx:rotation parses the term it is given rather than trusting a JSON number to survive the store.
_initialNote: The board before any tick runs. Every pair of agents starts further apart than the larger of their two vision radii, which is what makes turn 1's belief maps all-null. goblin-3 carries the seeded starvation mass — see _designNote.whyGoblin3StartsAlmostEmpty.

expectedTape.why: Nobody is inside anybody's vision radius, so every belief map is all-null and every chain falls through to its last rung. A predator with nothing in view wanders rather than holding still.

Two prey drift within 3 of each other, so each now appears in the other's belief map with a real cell. No rung in either chain reads another prey, so nothing about the turn changes. Belief and behaviour are separate, and this is the turn that proves it.
First multiple of foodSpawnIntervalTurns, so crumb-1 is minted at a seeded pick among open cells. It lands after every agent has already decided, so no one forages this turn.

goblin-1 now believes crumb-1 and runs findActionPath to its cell. Its plan is at least two directions long, which is what separates a real search result from a one-ply greedy step, and it takes only plan[0] this turn.

goblin-1 arrives on crumb-1's cell and the pass eats it, adding spawnedFoodMass. The fox has already acquired goblin-1 by now and is on the chase rung: the crumb draws the prey into the predator's radius, which is the shape the board is built for. Turn 5 is also the first multiple of preySpawnIntervalTurns, so goblin-4 arrives at the perimeter; a prey that spawns during the pass makes no decision until the next turn, so it has no rung here.

The chase closes. goblin-1 now believes the fox and flips from forage to evade mid-pursuit, which is the priority chain doing its job with no event system anywhere: the rung is recomputed from belief every turn, so a threat coming into view simply outranks food. crumb-2 is minted at the second multiple of foodSpawnIntervalTurns and goes unclaimed, because the prey that would have taken it is running.

goblin-1 believes crumb-2 and the fox on the same tick. Rung 1 beats rung 2 with no arbitration code anywhere: the chain is ordered, so the forage it would otherwise run is simply never reached. Its goal line flips to evading in the same tick its belief map changes.

The player places morsel-1 on a cell adjacent to the fox, with player provenance rather than the world tag, so "who put that there?" grounds. Nothing marks it as a trap. Prey walk the food class chain, so a morsel reads exactly as a crumb does and only distance separates them.

goblin-1 is backed against the house terrace, so every cell it can reach scores the same Chebyshev distance from the fox or worse. Evade holds it still, and the fox steps onto it. goblin-1 is on the evade rung for this turn's decision and off the board by the end of it, so it has no entry from turn 10 on. A follow camera tracking it falls back to overhead with a status line naming what happened; picking another agent resumes follow. crumb-3 is minted at the third multiple of foodSpawnIntervalTurns.

goblin-2 reaches morsel-1 and eats it, gaining placedFoodMass. It forages rather than evades because the fox, having taken goblin-1 on turn 9, now sees nothing at all and is back on the wander rung: a predator with an empty belief map keeps moving rather than standing still. goblin-3's mass reaches 0 and it starves, which is why it was seeded almost empty. Turn 10 is the second multiple of preySpawnIntervalTurns.
